R.|date=1977-11-11|title=New taxa and a new combination in the genus Cotyledon|url=https://journals.abcjournal.aosis.co.za/index.php/abc/article/view/1394|journal=Bothalia|volume=12|issue=2|pages=191–194|doi=10.4102/abc.v12i2.1394|issn=2311-9284|doi-access=free}} (possible ''[[Nomen illegitimum|nom. illeg.]]'',{{Cite web|website=International Crassulaceae Network|url=http://www.crassulaceae.ch/de/artikel?akID=29&aaID=2&aiID=T&aID=2256|title=TOMENTOSA ssp. * LADYSMITHENSIS (von Poellnitz) Tölken, 1977|first=Magrit|last=Bischofberger|access-date=2020-05-30}} see {{slink||Taxonomy}}) }} }} '''''Cotyledon tomentosa''''' is a [[species]] of [[flowering plant]] in the [[family (botany)|family]] [[Crassulaceae]], native to [[South Africa]]. It is a [[succulent]] [[evergreen]] shrub with large chunky ovate fuzzy green leaves. Its autonymous subspecies is known as the '''''bear's paw''''' because of the prominent "teeth" at the tips of its leaves. It forms large orange bell-shaped flowers in spring. In its native habitat, the [[Little Karoo]] region of South Africa, ''Cotyledons'' usually grow in rocky quartz fields where they have excellent drainage provided by very porous soil. == Description == [[File:Cotyledon tomentosa Berkeley CA .jpg|thumb|Tomentose leaves and flowers|left|alt=Tomentose leaves and flowers of ''C. tomentosa'' subsp. ''tomentosa'']] ''Cotyledon tomentosa'' is a perennial evergreen shrub, which is a member of the [[Crassulaceae]] family of succulent flowering plants. ''C. tomentosa'' has red, orange, or yellow bell-shaped flowers between July and September, and there are two recognized subspecies, subsp. ''tomentosa'' and subsp. ''ladismithiensis''. ''C. tomentosa'' subsp. ''tomentosa'', the [[Autonym (botany)|autonymous subspecies]], is a small, freely branched shrublet that grows to 70 cm tall. It has chunky green [[tomentose]] leaves that are [[oblanceolate]] to [[Oblong (botany)|oblong]], with 3-8 reddish teeth at the end. The other subspecies, subsp. ''ladismithiensis'', features long cylindrical leaves that generally do not have teeth. Subsp. ''ladismithiensis'' also tends to be smaller and less branched than subsp. ''tomentosa''. Finally, subsp. ''ladismithiensis'' has brown peeling bark, compared to the green hairy branches of subsp. ''tomentosa''. {{multiple image | align = left | direction = vertical | caption_align = center | header = Leaf shape comparison | image1 = | alt1 = ''C. tomentosa'' subsp. ''tomentosa'' | caption1 = subsp. ''tomentosa'' | image2 = Cotyledon tomentosa subsp ladismithiensis (cropped, leaf shape).jpg | alt2 = ''C. tomentosa'' subsp. ''ladismithiensis'' | caption2 = subsp. ''ladismithiensis'' | total_width = }} ==Taxonomy== ''Cotyledon tomentosa'' was described in 1862 by William Henry Harvey, and has no synonyms. ''Cotyledon tomentosa'' subsp. ''ladismithiensis'' was first described in 1907 by botanist [[Selmar Schonland]], who named it ''Cotyledon heterophylla''. Schonland noted that ''C. heterophylla'' seemed "more robust than ''C. tomentosa'', Harv. to which it is probably nearly allied." Schonland also cautioned that the differences he noted between ''C. heterophylla'' and ''C. tomentosa'' "to be used with great caution" as "relative characters [in the genus ''Cotyledon''] are frequently inconstant." However, the name ''C. heterophylla'' was a ''[[nomen illegitimum]]'', because it had already been applied in 1824 by [[William Roxburgh]] to what is now called ''Kalanchoe lanceolata''.{{Cite web|title=Cotyledon heterophylla Roxb. |website=Plants of the World Online |url=http://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:272673-1|access-date=2020-06-19}} In 1936, Karl von Poellnitz noted the conflict and gave the taxon a new name, ''Cotyledon ladysmithiensis'', for its native range near the town of [[Ladismith]], South Africa.{{Cite book|last1=Eggli|first1=Urs|title=Etymological Dictionary of Succulent Plant Names|last2=Newton|first2=Leonard E.|date=2004|publisher=Springer Berlin Heidelberg|isbn=978-3-642-05597-3|location=Berlin, Heidelberg|language=en|doi=10.1007/978-3-662-07125-0|s2cid=35535824}} [[Hellmut R. Toelken]] reclassified the taxon in 1977 as a subspecies, ''Cotyledon tomentosa'' subsp. ''ladismithiensis'', retaining a different spelling of von Poellnitz's name. This is the current accepted name of the subspecies, as listed on [[Plants of the World Online]]. According to Magrit Bischofberger, von Poellnitz's original spelling should be used according to Article 60.1 of the ''[[International Code of Nomenclature for algae, fungi, and plants|International Code of Nomenclature]]'', which states a name should not be changed even if it contains a spelling discrepancy (i.e. Ladismith vs. ''ladysmithiensis''). Another spelling variation used by the Illustrated Handbook of Succulent Plants is "''ladismithensis.''" [[File:Cotyledon tomentosa ssp ladysmithiensis.jpg|thumb|"''ladysmithiensis''" spelling used at the US Botanic Garden]] == Ecology == === Habitat and conservation === ''Cotyledon tomentosa'' is native to the semidesert [[Little Karoo]] region located in the southern parts of [[South Africa]], from [[Ladismith]] to [[Steytlerville]].{{Cite book|last=Court|first=Doreen|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=W6ZfOBb-QdsC|title=Succulent Flora of Southern Africa|date=2000-06-01|publisher=A. A. Balkema|isbn=978-90-5809-323-3|location=Rotterdam|pages=54, 93|language=en}} ''C. tomentosa'' subsp. ''tomentosa'' is found near [[Calitzdorp]], [[Willowmore]], and [[Steytlerville]], in the gravely soil of arid thicket, in slopes of sheltered ravines.{{Cite web|title=Cotyledon tomentosa Harv. subsp. tomentosa.|url=http://redlist.sanbi.org/species.php?species=3834-78|last1=Vlok|first1=J. H.|last2=Raimondo|first2=D.|date=2006|website=National Assessment: Red List of South African Plants version 2017.1.|access-date=2020-05-28}} In contrast, subsp. ''ladismithiensis'' is found in rocky outcrops in the southern [[Western Cape]],{{Cite web|title=Cotyledon tomentosa Harv. subsp. ladismithiensis (Poelln.) Toelken.|url=http://redlist.sanbi.org/species.php?species=3834-77|last1=Vlok|first1=J. H.|last2=Raimondo|first2=D.|date=2006|website=National Assessment: Red List of South African Plants version 2017.1.|access-date=2020-05-28}} between [[Laingsburg, Western Cape|Laingsburg]], [[Ladismith]], and Muiskraal. As of 2006, both subspecies are listed as vulnerable on the [[South African National Biodiversity Institute|SANBI]] Red List of South African Plants, because they have only been found in small subpopulations and are threatened by habitat degradation and [[Poaching|illegal gathering]] for the succulent trade. ''C. tomentosa'' subsp. ''tomentosa'' has only been found in five subpopulations, while subsp. ''ladismithiensis'' has only been found in seven subpopulations and has experienced a 10% decline in population over the past 90 years. === Toxicity === While ''C. tomentosa'' may be vulnerable to trampling by livestock, it is also known to be poisonous to livestock, dogs, and humans. ''Cotyledon'' species are known to contain [[cardiac glycoside]]s, including [[bufadienolide]]s,{{Cite journal|last1=S. Steyn|first1=Pieter|last2=R. van Heerden|first2=Fanie|date=1998|title=Bufadienolides of plant and animal origin|url=http://xlink.rsc.org/?DOI=a815397y|journal=Natural Product Reports|language=en|volume=15|issue=4|pages=397–413|doi=10.1039/a815397y|pmid=9736996|s2cid=30031690 |issn=0265-0568|url-access=subscription}} which are highly toxic to cattle, sheep, goats, and other livestock. The bufadienolides found in ''Cotyledon'' cause both acute and chronic poisoning.{{cite book |chapter=Diseases of the Cardiovascular System |date=2017 |url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/B9780702052460000103 |title=Veterinary Medicine |edition=eleventh |pages=657–715 |publisher=Elsevier |language=en |doi=10.1016/b978-0-7020-5246-0.00010-3 |isbn=978-0-7020-5246-0 |access-date=2020-05-28}} On the [[Toxicity class#World Health Organization|World Health Organization toxicity scale]], cardiac glycosides are considered Class Ia, "extremely hazardous,"{{cite book |last1=Smith |first1=Gideon F. |chapter=9: Biocultural Significance and Toxicity |date=2019-01-01 |url=http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/B9780128140079000098 |title=Kalanchoe (Crassulaceae) in Southern Africa |pages=105–110 |editor-last=Smith |editor-first=Gideon F. |publisher=Academic Press |language=en |isbn=978-0-12-814007-9 |access-date=2020-05-28 |last2=Figueiredo |first2=Estrela |last3=van Wyk |first3=Abraham E. |editor2-last=Figueiredo |editor2-first=Estrela |editor3-last=van Wyk |editor3-first=Abraham E.}} and a dose of only 1.0 g/kg body weight of a related species, ''[[Cotyledon orbiculata]]'', was lethal when fed to sheep.{{Cite journal|last=Botha|first=Christo J.|date=2013-11-18|title=Krimpsiekte in South Africa: Historical perspectives|url=https://jsava.co.za/index.php/jsava/article/view/1059|journal=Journal of the South African Veterinary Association|language=en|volume=84|issue=1|pages=5|doi=10.4102/jsava.v84i1.1059|issn=2224-9435|doi-access=free|hdl=2263/39710|hdl-access=free}} Bufadienolides are classified as [[neurotoxin]]s because they are strong inhibitors of [[sodium potassium pump]]s which are central to the function of animal nervous systems. Acute poisoning causes [[Arrhythmia|cardiac irregularity]] and [[heart failure]]. Other acute symptoms include apathy, hypersalivation, and tremors. Chronic poisoning in sheep and goats causes a [[Paraplegia|paraplegic]] disease known as krimpsiekte ("shrink disease" in [[Afrikaans]]), so named because poisoned individuals may arch their backs and [[Torticollis|bend their necks to one side]]. Krimpsiekte may have a mortality rate as high as 90%.{{Cite journal|last1=Botha|first1=C.J.|last2=Penrith|first2=M.-L.|date=October 2008|title=Poisonous plants of veterinary and human importance in southern Africa|journal=Journal of Ethnopharmacology|language=en|volume=119|issue=3|pages=549–558|doi=10.1016/j.jep.2008.07.022|pmid=18706990}} These toxins persist in the flesh of livestock afflicted with krimpsiekte, even after cooking, and dogs who consume this meat can exhibit similar neuromuscular symptoms.{{Cite journal|last=Botha|first=Christo|date=2016-03-16|title=Potential Health Risks Posed by Plant-Derived Cumulative Neurotoxic Bufadienolides in South Africa|journal=Molecules|language=en|volume=21|issue=3|pages=348|doi=10.3390/molecules21030348|issn=1420-3049|pmc=6273117|pmid=27102163|doi-access=free}} This secondary poisoning may also affect humans, but has not been thoroughly investigated. == Cultivation == [[File:Cotyledon tomentosa ladysmithiensis kz2.jpg|thumb|Variegated form]] In cultivation they thrive with bright light and ample airflow. Water thoroughly when soil is dry to the touch. Water with caution in winter, as the plant can lose its roots if the soil stays cold and wet for extended periods. They are dormant in summer. Protect from frost to prevent scarring.{{Cite web |title=Succulents :: Cotyledon tomentosa |website=GardenLife |url=http://www.gardenlife.com/store/Crassulaceae-Cotyledon-tomentosa.html|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110920164250/http://www.gardenlife.com/store/Crassulaceae-Cotyledon-tomentosa.html|archive-date=2011-09-20|access-date=2011-11-18}}{{Better source needed|date=September 2020}} In the UK ''Cotyledon tomentosa'' subsp. ''tomentosa'' has received the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]].{{cite web|title=''Cotyledon tomentosa'' subsp. ''tomentosa''|url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/327513/Cotyledon-tomentosa-subsp-tomentosa/Details|access-date=5 May 2020|publisher=RHS}} It does not tolerate temperatures below {{convert|5|C|F|abbr=on}}, so in [[temperate climate|temperate]] zones must be protected with glass throughout the winter months. However, it may be placed in a warm, sunny position outside during summer. ==References== {{Reflist}} ==Further reading== {{Commons category|Cotyledon tomentosa}} * {{Cite book|last1=van Jaarsveld|first1=Ernst J.|last2=Koutnik|first2=Daryl|title=Cotyledon and Tylecodon|date=2004|publisher=Umdaus Press|others=Illustrated by Elise Bodley and Lisa Strachan.|isbn=1-919766-32-4|location=Hatfield, South Africa|oclc=58463060}} {{Clear}} {{Taxonbar|from=Q3448252}} [[Category:Crassulaceae]] [[Category:Taxa named by William Henry Harvey]]
